{"artifact":"SmeDossierEnvelope","schema_version":"0.4.0","stage_id":"02.dossier_sections","probe":"rdmv-nj-d","lineage":{"input_manifest_sha256":"968e0252c007f9c7f19a81a73637eb939765f836b861ed0fccd33e811541318a","candidate_lineage_id":"2026-10-28-rdmv-nj-class-d:lineage:37","source_registry_sha256":"057b72c7c679c997f56ae00ef97a6b14dbe264551f4121b9bf67b0457d9cf7c1","source_liveness_sha256":"1ca7bfbb9e3c0a6b19e5e808ecab6fe8329f3b4799e394abc260d65c1d6513e7"},"envelope_scope":{"kind":"partial_chunk","assigned_section_ids":["C"],"chunk_index":1,"chunk_total":1},"section_char_limit":12000,"sections":[{"section_id":"C","chunk_id":"C.01","merge_seq":1,"domain":"Defensive driving: night driving, driving situations, emergencies, vehicle failures and crashes","heading":"C — Defensive driving: night stopping distances and headlight rules, city and highway driving, road hazards and work zones, skids and emergency stops, fires, water and railroad tracks, vehicle failures, crash avoidance and crash reporting","learner_facing":true,"markdown":"## C — Defensive driving: night stopping distances and headlight rules, city and highway driving, road hazards and work zones, skids and emergency stops, fires, water and railroad tracks, vehicle failures, crash avoidance and crash reporting
Knowledge domain: how a New Jersey driver adjusts for darkness, city streets, highways, hazards and work zones, how to react when the vehicle skids, leaves the pavement, catches fire, enters water, stalls on tracks or suffers a mechanical failure, how to choose the least harmful outcome when a crash is coming, and what the law requires after a crash.

FACT_ID: sec09-F01 | anchor: A01
Roughly 90 percent of the decisions a driver makes depend on what they can see, and that vision shrinks after dark. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0102]

FACT_ID: sec09-F02 | anchor: A01
At night, slow down and stay within the reach of your headlights so the vehicle can always stop inside the distance you can actually see. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0102]

FACT_ID: sec09-F03 | anchor: A01
The manual's night stopping table assumes low beams and a nighttime reaction time of 1.5 seconds, and notes that a vehicle covers 88 feet each second at 60 mph. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0102]

FACT_ID: sec09-F04 | anchor: A01
On low beams at 20 mph, the table lists 44 feet of reaction distance plus 31 feet of braking distance, for 75 feet of total stopping distance. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0102]

FACT_ID: sec09-F05 | anchor: A01
On low beams at 40 mph, the table lists 88 feet of reaction distance plus 123 feet of braking distance, for 211 feet in total. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0102]

FACT_ID: sec09-F06 | anchor: A01
On low beams at 60 mph, the table lists 132 feet of reaction distance plus 277 feet of braking distance, for 409 feet in total. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0102]

FACT_ID: sec09-F07 | anchor: A02
Headlights belong on at dusk, at night, at dawn, on dark days, and any time weather cuts visibility to under 500 feet. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0103]

FACT_ID: sec09-F08 | anchor: A02
New Jersey law requires headlights to be on whenever the windshield wipers are running. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0103]

FACT_ID: sec09-F09 | anchor: A02
In a crosswalk, pedestrians and people using wheelchairs or mobility-assistance vehicles always have the right of way, and drivers must stop for pedestrians whether or not the crosswalk is marked. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0103]

FACT_ID: sec09-F10 | anchor: A02
Scan at least 12 seconds ahead, meaning you should spot objects far enough away that reaching them would take at least 12 seconds. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0103]

FACT_ID: sec09-F11 | anchor: A02
On a clear city street at 25 mph, looking that far ahead works out to seeing about one block in front of you. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0103]

FACT_ID: sec09-F12 | anchor: A02
Approaching an intersection, slow down, glance left and then right, and keep your foot on the brake; at the crosswalk itself the vehicle should be at its slowest. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0103]

FACT_ID: sec09-F13 | anchor: A03
An intersection with no lights or signs has no traffic control at all, even if the road is wide, smooth or busy, so avoiding a collision there is entirely up to the driver. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0104]

FACT_ID: sec09-F14 | anchor: A03
Going over the posted limit or too fast for conditions is among the most common factors in crashes, which happen on highways even in good weather on dry pavement. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0104]

FACT_ID: sec09-F15 | anchor: A03
Warning signs mark hazards such as hills, dips, narrow bridges, bumps and railroad tracks; slow down there, because speeding and then braking hard can cause a skid or a spin. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0104]

FACT_ID: sec09-F16 | anchor: A04
In New Jersey, fines for motor vehicle violations double when they are committed in a roadway construction zone. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0105]

FACT_ID: sec09-F17 | anchor: A04
A work zone is announced as far as one-half mile ahead of the work area, either by an advance warning sign or by a vehicle with flashing lights. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0105]

FACT_ID: sec09-F18 | anchor: A04
Work zone basics are to stay fully attentive, obey signs and flaggers, turn on headlights so workers can see you, avoid tailgating and keep to the posted speed limit. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0105]

FACT_ID: sec09-F19 | anchor: A05
An ignition system lets you remove the key only when the transmission is in Park. [A05]
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0106]

FACT_ID: sec09-F20 | anchor: A05
Never turn a steering-wheel ignition to the lock position while the vehicle is moving, because the steering locks as the vehicle turns and you lose control. [A05]
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0106]

FACT_ID: sec09-F21 | anchor: A05
Skids usually come from sudden turns, lane changes or hard braking, often on wet or icy roads, and are handled the same way in front-wheel and rear-wheel drive vehicles. [A05]
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0106]

FACT_ID: sec09-F22 | anchor: A05
If the rear of the vehicle slides, lift your foot off the gas and steer in the direction the rear is skidding without oversteering, while looking where you want to go. [A05]
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0106]

FACT_ID: sec09-F23 | anchor: A06
For an emergency stop on a highway with a paved shoulder, signal and move onto the shoulder at or near traffic speed before slowing; on an unpaved shoulder, slow to a safe speed before leaving the road. [A06]
Source: [A06 -> pdf-0107]

FACT_ID: sec09-F24 | anchor: A06
After stopping on the shoulder, set a flare or warning sign just behind the vehicle and another warning device at least 300 feet back, about 120 paces. [A06]
Source: [A06 -> pdf-0107]

FACT_ID: sec09-F25 | anchor: A06
If the wheels drift onto the shoulder, do not jerk back onto the pavement; stay on the shoulder, ease off the gas, and once at 25 mph or less turn the wheel one-quarter turn toward the road. [A06]
Source: [A06 -> pdf-0107]

FACT_ID: sec09-F26 | anchor: A07
Most car fires start with an electrical short circuit; get everyone out and away at once, call for help, and never try to fight the fire yourself. [A07]
Source: [A07 -> pdf-0108]

FACT_ID: sec09-F27 | anchor: A07
A vehicle with its windows and doors shut floats for about three to ten minutes, and the best escape is through an open window while it is still on the surface. [A07]
Source: [A07 -> pdf-0108]

FACT_ID: sec09-F28 | anchor: A07
If the vehicle stalls on railroad tracks, everyone must get out and move far from the vehicle and tracks even when no train is coming, then call the number on the Emergency Notification sign or 911. [A07]
Source: [A07 -> pdf-0108]

FACT_ID: sec09-F29 | anchor: A07
If a train is approaching, run away from the vehicle and tracks at a 45-degree angle toward the direction the train is coming from, to avoid flying debris. [A07]
Source: [A07 -> pdf-0108]

FACT_ID: sec09-F30 | anchor: A08
If conventional disc and drum brakes fail, downshift and then pump the pedal hard and quickly several times to try to build pressure. [A08]
Source: [A08 -> pdf-0109]

FACT_ID: sec09-F31 | anchor: A08
If pumping fails, use the parking brake while holding its release so you can let up if the rear wheels lock and the vehicle starts to skid. [A08]
Source: [A08 -> pdf-0109]

FACT_ID: sec09-F32 | anchor: A08
With a flat or blowout, grip the wheel firmly, keep the vehicle straight, take your foot off the gas without braking, and coast to a stop in a safe spot. [A08]
Source: [A08 -> pdf-0109]

FACT_ID: sec09-F33 | anchor: A09
If the gas pedal sticks, keep your eyes on the road, shift quickly to neutral, steer to a safe spot off the road, and turn off the engine. [A09]
Source: [A09 -> pdf-0110]

FACT_ID: sec09-F34 | anchor: A09
If the hood flies up, slow down at once, look under the hood or out the side window, and use the center line or lane markings to guide the vehicle off the road. [A09]
Source: [A09 -> pdf-0110]

FACT_ID: sec09-F35 | anchor: A09
When a collision threatens, the three choices are to stop, to turn or to speed up. [A09]
Source: [A09 -> pdf-0110]

FACT_ID: sec09-F36 | anchor: A09
With antilock brakes, press as hard as needed and keep steering without pumping; with conventional brakes, pump them to keep steering control, since holding them down hard locks the wheels. [A09]
Source: [A09 -> pdf-0110]

FACT_ID: sec09-F37 | anchor: A10
If a crash looks likely, steer away from oncoming traffic even if that means leaving the road, and choose to hit something that gives way, such as shrubs, rather than something hard. [A10]
Source: [A10 -> pdf-0111]

FACT_ID: sec09-F38 | anchor: A10
When something must be hit, prefer an object moving your way over a stationary one, and a stationary one over one coming head-on, aiming for a glancing blow. [A10]
Source: [A10 -> pdf-0111]

FACT_ID: sec09-F39 | anchor: A11
If you are about to be hit head-on while wearing a shoulder strap in a car with airbags, protect your face with your arms and hands. [A11]
Source: [A11 -> pdf-0112]

FACT_ID: sec09-F40 | anchor: A12
New Jersey requires drivers to notify police of any crash involving injury, death, or vehicle or property damage, and a body must not be moved until police or an ambulance arrive. [A12]
Source: [A12 -> pdf-0113]

FACT_ID: sec09-F41 | anchor: A12
When property damage exceeds $500 or someone is injured, send a written report to the MVC within 10 days unless the police file one, and notify your insurer at once. [A12]
Source: [A12 -> pdf-0113]

Misconceptions: turning the ignition off while moving does not stop the car safely, it locks the steering; braking during a side skid or a blowout makes things worse; a quiet road with no signals is not protected; a burning car is not something to put out yourself; jerking the wheel to get off the shoulder causes a slingshot into traffic.
Mnemonics: night table goes seventy-five, two-eleven, four-oh-nine feet at twenty, forty and sixty; stop, turn or speed up; off the shoulder at a quarter turn once at or under twenty-five; run toward the train at an angle; give way, same direction, still, never head-on.
Glossary: reaction distance means ground covered before the brake is pressed; braking distance means ground needed to bring the vehicle to a full stop; uncontrolled intersection means a crossing with no lights or signs; work zone means a road construction area announced by an advance warning sign; glancing blow means a sideswipe instead of a direct hit.
Dynamic facts: the nationwide work zone crash statistics and the property damage threshold for written crash reports can change; confirm them on official New Jersey and federal websites.
